newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek finmin criticised for FRN private placement.
newsitem.headline: Greek finmin criticised for FRN private placement.

text.p: The Greek finance ministry has been accused of discriminatory bank selection practices that hurt the secondary bond market and raise the cost of state borrowing with its recent private placement of state securities.
Dealers said on Wednesday the state privately placed 7-year FRNs at par worth 830 billion drachmas carrying an annual coupon of 14.20 percent with some local state and private banks.
The finance ministry has yet to issue a statement outlining the terms of the deal, but government and commercial bank sources have confirmed them.
"The finance ministry mishandled the private placement of FRNs and T-bills and this is going to backfire," said a senior money market dealer at a foreign bank.
"The lack of transperancy will raise the cost of state borrowing and hurt the secondary market."

The trader said the market was bullish following a national election win by the ruling socialist government over the weekend and the state could have ended up getting better bids from banks via a large scale auction.
"The sentiment was bullish after the elections and the treasury could have paid much less for borrowing the same amount via an auction," he said.
The socialists won a comfortable majority of 162 seats in the 300-seat parliament in Sunday's elections. The financial markets had anticipated the outcome.

"What is this," asked another dealer at a foreign bank. "I had brokers call me about this September FRN which I was unaware of and ask me for prices. Is this the right way for a ministry to dessiminate important information to the market?".

The local banks involved in the deal, state National Bank, Commercial Bank, Ionian Bank and private Alpha Credit Bank and Ergo Bank, held an expiring five-year FRN issued in 1991 that carried no spread over the 12-month benchmark 12-month T-bill.

Market players and press reports said these banks received a gross commission of 220 basis points for the private placement of FRN, much higher than the normal 110 basis points. This infuriated other Greek and foreign banks.
Some foreign banks took quotes for the seven-year FRNs off their screens on Thursday in protest against the finance ministry's policy on the private placement issue.

But dealers at the participating banks said the bigger commission was justified. They noted losses incurred by holding on to a jumbo five-year FRN carrying no spread over the 12-month T-bill benchmark issued by the treasury in 1991 and expiring on September 30.

Traders at the protesting banks counter-attacked by saying that the treasury could have compensated the banks for their losses in the form of a cash subsidy instead of messing around with the secondary bond market, liquidity and interest rates.
Some traders even suggested there was an implicit accord among participating banks not to let FRNs prices fall below a particular level.

"What is really worrisome is that the officials who took the initiative and put together the private placement deal do not seem to understand the market implications of their actions," said a dealer at a foreign bank.
He added that market distortions could have been avoided if participating banks were asked to keep the FRNs on their books instead of selling them to the market.
